dialogue_quality_notes: Repeated framing phrase 'whoever cooks washes their pan' appears across rounds and serves as the central rule proposal.
Participants give concise, concrete reasons (need to sleep, getting home late, buying supplies) that guided allocation.
Resolution proceeded by straightforward proposal-and-assignment rather than prolonged debate; language is natural and cooperative.
evaluation.final_reason: The group agreed both a behavioral rule and an allocation of weeknights: A verbally accepted responsibility to wash the pan ('Okay, I'll wash it now') and all participants agreed 'whoever cooks washes their pan.' They also set a rota for weeknight stove use with named nights: 'Okay — rota's set: Agent C Tuesday, Agent D Wednesday, Agent B Thursday. Whoever cooks washes their pan.' This mutual assignment resolved the scheduling incompatibility and the cleaning responsibility.
position_change_notes: Agent A: initially defensive but agreed to wash the pan immediately and accepted a rota ('Okay, I'll wash it now.'; 'Okay, rota sounds fair.').
Agent B: pressed for immediate action and then accepted the proposed rule and took Thursday ('Whoever cooks washes their pan works for me...'; 'I can take Thursday nights.').
Agent C: reported the unwashed pan, accepted the rule and volunteered Tuesday ('Okay — whoever cooks washes their pan. Agent A, thanks for agreeing to wash yours now.'; 'I can take Tuesday nights.').

Agent D: introduced the scheduling conflict due to late arrival and proposed a rota, then took Wednesday ('I usually get home late and can't use the stove on weeknights. Can we do a simple rota...'; 'I'll take Wednesday nights.').

round_scores.evidence: Agent A defensive: 'Don't call me out like this — can we agree whoever cooks washes their pan, or else set a rota?' Agent B demands immediate action: 'Agent A, can you wash yours now? The smell's already in the corridor and I need to sleep early.' The kitchen-usage/cleanliness dispute is explicit and not settled by the end of the round.

Agent A agrees to wash now: 'Okay, I'll wash it now.' Both A and B accept the rule 'whoever cooks washes their pan.' The immediate complaint about the unwashed pan is addressed verbally, but scheduling/rota and stove-use timing issues remain unresolved.

Agent D introduces a new substantive incompatibility about stove availability: 'I usually get home late and can't use the stove on weeknights. Can we do a simple rota so each person has at least one weeknight?' This creates an unresolved allocation conflict over weeknight stove use.

Agent A accepts the rota idea and asks for specific nights: 'Agent D — which weeknight can you take? Agent C and Agent B, pick nights too so we can set it now.' Agent B volunteers Thursday. Progress toward resolution, but not all nights assigned yet.
Agent C takes Tuesday: 'I can take Tuesday nights.' The rota is partially filled (B: Thursday, C: Tuesday) but one person's night remains to be assigned; the scheduling conflict is not fully settled.

Agent D takes Wednesday: 'I'll take Wednesday nights.' Agent A summarizes the agreement: 'Okay — rota's set: Agent C Tuesday, Agent D Wednesday, Agent B Thursday. Whoever cooks washes their pan.' All introduced substantive issues (washing responsibility and weeknight stove allocation) are explicitly assigned.

substantive_insights: Two distinct but related problems drove the discussion: immediate cleanliness (unwashed pan and smells) and recurring practical access to the stove (weeknight timings).
The eventual solution combined a behavioral rule (responsibility for washing) with a time-allocation scheme (simple rota), addressing both cleanliness and access.
Agents provided pragmatic trade-offs (taking specific nights) rather than demanding others change long-standing habits, which enabled a quick settlement.
